claim: Lifespan transcriptome trajectories describe a calendar of gene regulatory events in the brain of humans and mice.
source: We found that lifespan transcriptome trajectories describe a calendar of gene regulatory events in the brain of humans and mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including transcriptome analysis across the lifespan.

claim: Transcriptome trajectories defined a sequence of gene expression changes in neuronal, glial and endothelial cell-types.
source: Transcriptome trajectories defined a sequence of gene expression changes in neuronal, glial and endothelial cell-types, which enabled prediction of age from tissue samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cell-type enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3 and described in the Results section.

claim: Transcriptome trajectories enabled prediction of age from tissue samples.
source: Transcriptome trajectories defined a sequence of gene expression changes in neuronal, glial and endothelial cell-types, which enabled prediction of age from tissue samples.
evidence: This is supported by the age prediction analysis using support vector machines shown in Figure 2i,j with R² values of 0.88 for humans and 0.94 for mice.

claim: A major lifespan landmark was the peak change in trajectories occurring in humans at 26 years of age.
source: A major lifespan landmark was the peak change in trajectories occurring in humans at 26 years and in mice at 5 months of age.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the TTTP analysis shown in Figure 2a, which shows a sharp peak at mean age of 26.0 years in males.

claim: A major lifespan landmark was the peak change in trajectories occurring in mice at 5 months of age.
source: A major lifespan landmark was the peak change in trajectories occurring in humans at 26 years and in mice at 5 months of age.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the TTTP analysis shown in Figure 2c, which shows a peak at mean age of 156 days (approximately 5 months) in male mice.

claim: The species-conserved peak in transcriptome trajectories was delayed in females.
source: This species-conserved peak was delayed in females and marked a reorganization of expression of synaptic and schizophrenia-susceptibility genes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a for humans (27.5 years in females vs 26.0 years in males, p=0) and Figure 2c for mice (165 days in females vs 156 days in males, p<1×10−323).

claim: The peak in transcriptome trajectories marked a reorganization of expression of synaptic genes.
source: This species-conserved peak was delayed in females and marked a reorganization of expression of synaptic and schizophrenia-susceptibility genes.
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis of PSD genes shown in Figure 4, demonstrating significant enrichment of synaptic genes during the young adult peak.

claim: The peak in transcriptome trajectories marked a reorganization of expression of schizophrenia-susceptibility genes.
source: This species-conserved peak was delayed in females and marked a reorganization of expression of synaptic and schizophrenia-susceptibility genes.
evidence: This is supported by the enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5, demonstrating significant enrichment of schizophrenia susceptibility genes at 22-26 years.

claim: The lifespan calendar predicted the characteristic age of onset in young adults for schizophrenia.
source: The lifespan calendar predicted the characteristic age of onset in young adults and sex differences in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ALiGeT enrichment window for schizophrenia genes spanning 22-26 years (Figure 5a), which corresponds to the clinically reported age of onset.

claim: The lifespan calendar predicted sex differences in schizophrenia.
source: The lifespan calendar predicted the characteristic age of onset in young adults and sex differences in schizophrenia.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b where the ALiGeT enrichment window was significantly earlier in males (20-26 years) than females (26-28 years), p=4.7×10−14.

claim: Cognition, emotion and personality emerge progressively during childhood and adolescence, with executive functions peaking in early adulthood.
source: Longitudinal studies show cognition, emotion and personality emerge progressively during childhood and adolescence, with executive functions peaking in early adulthood (Craik and Bialystok, 2006; De Luca et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous longitudinal studies.

claim: Most psychiatric disorders arise during later stages of brain development in the teenage years and early twenties.
source: This coincides with the onset of some of the most devastating psychiatric disorders, most of which arise during later stages of brain development in the teenage years and early twenties (Kessler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kessler et al., 2007.

claim: Impulse-control disorders arise in late childhood and early teen years.
source: For example, impulse-control disorders arise in late childhood and early teen years, substance abuse peaks in the early twenties, and schizophrenia in the mid-twenties (with a delay of around two years in females) (Häfner et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Häfner et al., 1993.

claim: Substance abuse peaks in the early twenties.
source: For example, impulse-control disorders arise in late childhood and early teen years, substance abuse peaks in the early twenties, and schizophrenia in the mid-twenties (with a delay of around two years in females) (Häfner et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Häfner et al., 1993.

claim: Schizophrenia onset occurs in the mid-twenties with a delay of around two years in females.
source: For example, impulse-control disorders arise in late childhood and early teen years, substance abuse peaks in the early twenties, and schizophrenia in the mid-twenties (with a delay of around two years in females) (Häfner et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Häfner et al., 1993.

claim: The age of onset for schizophrenia has a heritability estimated at 33%.
source: However, the finding that the age of onset for schizophrenia has a heritability estimated at 33% (Hare et al., 2010), suggests that the timing may have a genetic basis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hare et al., 2010.

claim: Many schizophrenia mutations directly impact on synapse proteins, particularly those involved with postsynaptic signalling mechanisms in excitatory synapses.
source: It is widely accepted that many mutations directly impact on synapse proteins, particularly those involved with postsynaptic signalling mechanisms in excitatory synapses (Kirov et al., 2008; Pocklington et al., 2015; Fromer et al., 2014; Fernández et al., 2009a; Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: PSD95 supercomplexes play a major role in regulating cognitive functions.
source: The postsynaptic proteome of excitatory synapses is physically organised into multiprotein complexes of which the supercomplexes assembled by PSD95 (Husi et al., 2000; Frank et al., 2016a; Frank and Grant, 2017; Frank et al., 2017) play a major role in regulating cognitive functions (Migaud et al., 1998; Nithianantharajah et al., 2013) and are disrupted by schizophrenia mutations (Pocklington et al., 2015; Fromer et al., 2014; Fernández et al., 2009a; Singh et al., 2017; Kirov et al., 2012; Purcell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: PSD95 supercomplexes are disrupted by schizophrenia mutations.
source: The postsynaptic proteome of excitatory synapses is physically organised into multiprotein complexes of which the supercomplexes assembled by PSD95 (Husi et al., 2000; Frank et al., 2016a; Frank and Grant, 2017; Frank et al., 2017) play a major role in regulating cognitive functions (Migaud et al., 1998; Nithianantharajah et al., 2013) and are disrupted by schizophrenia mutations (Pocklington et al., 2015; Fromer et al., 2014; Fernández et al., 2009a; Singh et al., 2017; Kirov et al., 2012; Purcell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcriptome profiling of the brain at different ages has shown complex changes in expression levels across the lifespan.
source: Transcriptome profiling of the brain at different ages has shown complex changes in expression levels across the lifespan (Colantuoni et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colantuoni et al., 2011.

claim: In early onset brain disorders such as intellectual disability and autism, gene expression levels in fetal and early postnatal development correlate with enrichment in autism susceptibility genes.
source: In early onset brain disorders, such as intellectual disability and autism, gene expression levels in fetal and early postnatal development correlate with enrichment in autism susceptibility genes (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Willsey et al., 2013 and Parikshak et al., 2013.

claim: Correlation based approaches are unable to account for the full complexity of transcriptional changes that occur with age.
source: However, correlation based approaches (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013; Gulsuner et al., 2013) (e.g. weighted gene coexpression network analysis) are unable to account for the full complexity of transcriptional changes that occur with age.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous methods, supported by citations and the development of new methods (TTTP, DeGeT, ALiGeT) in this manuscript.

claim: TTTPs were sharply concentrated during early adulthood in humans.
source: Although TTTPs were identified across the lifespan, they were sharply concentrated during early adulthood.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 2a showing a sharp peak in TTTP frequency during early adulthood.

claim: The mean age of TTTPs was 26.0 years in human males and 27.5 years in human females.
source: Summing the number at each age shows a striking peak and a mean of 26.0 years in males and 27.5 years in females (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0, Figure 2a, example trajectories with different turning points shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2a with statistical significance.

claim: The sex difference in TTTP peak age was statistically significant (p=0).
source: Summing the number at each age shows a striking peak and a mean of 26.0 years in males and 27.5 years in females (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0, Figure 2a, example trajectories with different turning points shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with the statistical test result.

claim: Removing X-chromosome genes from the analysis had no effect on the sex difference in TTTP peak age.
source: Removing X-chromosome genes from the analysis had no effect on this sex difference (p=0).
evidence: This is a control analysis demonstrating that the sex difference is not due to X-chromosome genes.

claim: Mouse hippocampus showed a peak in TTTPs with a mean of 156 days for males and 165 days for females.
source: To determine whether this TTTP-peak was human specific, we performed an equivalent analysis using transcriptome data from the hippocampus of 186 mice of both sexes between 58 and 600 days of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 2): this also revealed a peak in the frequency of TTTPs with a mean of 156 days for male and 165 days for female mice (p<1×10−323, Figure 2c).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 2c with statistical significance.

claim: The sex difference in mouse TTTP peak age was statistically significant (p<1×10−323).
source: To determine whether this TTTP-peak was human specific, we performed an equivalent analysis using transcriptome data from the hippocampus of 186 mice of both sexes between 58 and 600 days of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 2): this also revealed a peak in the frequency of TTTPs with a mean of 156 days for male and 165 days for female mice (p<1×10−323, Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated with the statistical test result.

claim: Mouse postnatal day 156 (5 months) is equivalent to human early adulthood based on equivalent levels of cortical synaptic maturation.
source: Although there is a lack of previous research on the age equivalence of early adulthood between rodents and humans, our results are concordant with estimations made using the TranslatingTime species comparison model which suggests that p156 (5 months) is equivalent to human early adulthood based on equivalent levels of cortical synaptic maturation (Pinto et al., 2015; Pinto et al., 2013; Workman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the TranslatingTime model studies.

claim: 90% of TTTPs occur by 40 years of age in humans.
source: Plotting the cumulative distribution of TTTPs across the lifespan further illustrates the TTTP-peak in young adults (Figure 2d,e), and shows that 90% of TTTPs occur by 40 years of age, corresponding to the last stages of human brain development (De Luca et al., 2003; Lebel et al., 2012; Wood et al., 2004) and 7 months of age in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2d with citations to brain development studies.

claim: 90% of TTTPs occur by 7 months of age in mice.
source: Plotting the cumulative distribution of TTTPs across the lifespan further illustrates the TTTP-peak in young adults (Figure 2d,e), and shows that 90% of TTTPs occur by 40 years of age, corresponding to the last stages of human brain development (De Luca et al., 2003; Lebel et al., 2012; Wood et al., 2004) and 7 months of age in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Humans and mice share a lifespan program of brain gene expression with conserved features despite greatly differing lifespans.
source: These data indicate that despite greatly differing lifespans, these two mammalian species share a lifespan program of brain gene expression with conserved features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of human and mouse TTTP data.

claim: TTTPs for genes with the greatest expression changes prior to the TTTP were concentrated around the late-twenties in humans.
source: As shown in Figure 2f, the TTTPs for genes with the greatest expression changes prior to the TTTP were concentrated around the late-twenties, reinforcing the earlier finding that this is a significant period for switching in the trajectories.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Upward inflecting genes were more common in young subjects (<25 years) and downward inflecting genes more common in older subjects (>40 years).
source: Next, we separated genes into those with upward or downward trajectories prior to the turning point: overall there were similar numbers in each category, although there was a skew toward upward inflecting genes being more common in young subjects (<25 years) and downward inflecting genes more common in older subjects (>40 years) (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The vast majority of probes had plateaued by 30 years of age.
source: The vast majority of probes had plateaued by 30 years of age.
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of post-TTTP trajectory behavior shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Young adulthood is a crucial time for switching brain gene expression and establishing the set points of most genes for later life.
source: Together these findings show that young adulthood is a crucial time for switching brain gene expression and establishing the set points of most genes for later life.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TTTP analysis showing concentration of turning points and plateaus in young adulthood.

claim: Classifiers trained on gene expression data predicted age in test sets with an accuracy of 5.5 years in humans.
source: To test this, we used radial basis support vector machines and demonstrated that classifiers trained on partitioned subsets of the gene expression data (training sets) predicted age in the test sets with an accuracy (defined as mean |AgeActual−AgePredicted|) in humans of 5.5 years and 28 days in mice.
evidence: This is stated based on the age prediction analysis using support vector machines.

claim: Classifiers trained on gene expression data predicted age in test sets with an accuracy of 28 days in mice.
source: To test this, we used radial basis support vector machines and demonstrated that classifiers trained on partitioned subsets of the gene expression data (training sets) predicted age in the test sets with an accuracy (defined as mean |AgeActual−AgePredicted|) in humans of 5.5 years and 28 days in mice.
evidence: This is stated based on the age prediction analysis using support vector machines.

claim: Age prediction classifiers showed accurate predictions across the entire range of ages in both humans (R² = 0.88) and mice (R² = 0.94).
source: Remarkably, they showed accurate age predictions across the entire range of ages in both species (human, R2 = 0.88, mice, R2 = 0.94) (Figure 2i,j) using only 40 probes in humans and 100 in mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated with R² values and shown in Figure 2i,j.

claim: Age prediction used only 40 probes in humans and 100 in mice.
source: Remarkably, they showed accurate age predictions across the entire range of ages in both species (human, R2 = 0.88, mice, R2 = 0.94) (Figure 2i,j) using only 40 probes in humans and 100 in mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A 'genetic lifespan calendar' of transcriptome events is a conserved feature of mammals.
source: Thus, TTTPs and trajectories are highly characteristic features defining brain age across the lifespan in mice and humans. This indicates a 'genetic lifespan calendar' of transcriptome events is a conserved feature of mammals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of human and mouse data showing conserved features.

claim: Most cellular changes occurred prior to 35 years of age with prominent neuronal changes in young adults.
source: Moreover, most of these changes occurred prior to 35 years of age with prominent neuronal changes in young adults.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the cell-type enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The enrichment of neuronal genes in the early adult peak is conserved across species and brain regions.
source: These findings show that the enrichment of neuronal genes in the early adult peak is conserved across species and brain regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing human neocortex and mouse hippocampus data.

claim: Genes with high PeGeT scores are enriched in Mammalian Phenotype Ontology annotations for behavioural phenotypes (p=7.5×10−05).
source: Mammalian Phenotype Ontology annotations indicated their roles in behavioural (p=7.5×10−05) and nervous system (p=0.0002) phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and represents functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes with high PeGeT scores are enriched in Mammalian Phenotype Ontology annotations for nervous system phenotypes (p=0.0002).
source: Mammalian Phenotype Ontology annotations indicated their roles in behavioural (p=7.5×10−05) and nervous system (p=0.0002) phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and represents functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Human postsynaptic density (hPSD) genes showed significantly higher PeGeT scores than expected by chance (p<0.0009).
source: To probe the synaptic role in more detail, we examined genes coding for proteins in the human postsynaptic density (hPSD) (Bayés et al., 2011) and the postsynaptic PSD95 supercomplexes (Husi et al., 2000; Frank et al., 2017; Fernández et al., 2009b; Frank et al., 2016b), which are crucial in controlling synaptic plasticity and behaviour: both sets showed significantly higher PeGeT scores than expected by chance (p<0.0009 and p=0.0019 respectively, Figure 4a,b, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: PSD95 supercomplex genes showed significantly higher PeGeT scores than expected by chance (p=0.0019).
source: To probe the synaptic role in more detail, we examined genes coding for proteins in the human postsynaptic density (hPSD) (Bayés et al., 2011) and the postsynaptic PSD95 supercomplexes (Husi et al., 2000; Frank et al., 2017; Fernández et al., 2009b; Frank et al., 2016b), which are crucial in controlling synaptic plasticity and behaviour: both sets showed significantly higher PeGeT scores than expected by chance (p<0.0009 and p=0.0019 respectively, Figure 4a,b, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Human PSD genes showed a window of increased ALiGeT scores during young adulthood (22-33 years) in the Braincloud dataset.
source: To establish the age window when synaptic genes showed TTTPs, we used a bootstrapping approach to test whether synaptic genes have higher ALiGeT scores in particular years in the Braincloud dataset. Each year between 22 and 33 years of age showed a significant increase in synapse-associated ALiGeT scores and we refer to this as the ALiGeThPSD window.
evidence: This is stated with the age range and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Human PSD genes showed a window of increased ALiGeT scores during young adulthood (17-22 years) in the Somel dataset.
source: A replication study (Somel) using a smaller human transcriptome dataset (Somel et al., 2009) gave an overlapping estimate for the synaptic ALiGeThPSD window at 17–22 years (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated with the age range and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: All five consecutive age sets from 24 to 36 years were significantly enriched in hPSD genes using the DeGeT method.
source: We next applied the DeGeT method and found all five consecutive age sets from 24 to 36 years were significantly enriched in hPSD genes (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The ALiGeTmPSD window in mice was identified at 126 to 151 days.
source: Similarly, we identified the ALiGeTmPSD window in mice at 126 to 151 days (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Transcripts encoding postsynaptic proteins were significantly enriched in TTTPs during early adulthood in all four datasets tested, spanning two species and two brain regions.
source: These data show that transcripts encoding postsynaptic proteins were significantly enriched in TTTPs during early adulthood in all four datasets tested, spanning two species and two brain regions.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the analysis of Braincloud, Somel, BrainSpan, and mouse hippocampus datasets.

claim: The majority of Ca2+- and Na+/K+-ATPases detected in the mouse synaptosome dataset were affected by aging.
source: Amongst the affected channels were the majority of Ca2+- and Na+/K+-ATPases detected in our dataset, including three of the subunits of Atp2b (often referred to as PMCA).
evidence: This is stated based on the proteomic analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Aged rodents have decreased Ca2+- and Na+/K+- ATPase activity.
source: This finding recapitulates and extends the previous reports that aged rodents have decreased Ca2+- and Na+/K+- ATPase activity (Zaidi et al., 1998; Tanaka and Ando, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Postsynaptic proteins have been linked to the genetic susceptibility of schizophrenia.
source: Prompted by previous results showing that postsynaptic proteins have been linked to the genetic susceptibility of schizophrenia (Fromer et al., 2014; Fernández et al., 2009a; Nithianantharajah et al., 2013; Kirov et al., 2012; Purcell et al., 2014), we hypothesized that TTTPs may be relevant to the age of onset of schizophrenia.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The ALiGeTscz enrichment window for schizophrenia susceptibility genes spanned 22–26 years.
source: The ALiGeTscz enrichment window spanned 22–26 years (Figure 5a) corresponding to the clinically reported age of onset defined by the first episode of psychotic symptoms and window of maximum vulnerability (Kessler et al., 2007; Häfner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with the age range and shown in Figure 5a, with citations to clinical studies.

claim: The ALiGeTscz enrichment window was significantly earlier in males (20–26 years) than females (26–28 years) with Wilcoxon p=4.7×10−14.
source: Since males are reported to have an earlier disease onset than females (Kessler et al., 2007), we tested males and females separately and found the ALiGeTscz enrichment window was significantly earlier in males than females (males 20–26 years, females 26–28 years; wilcoxon p=4.7×10−14, Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: DeGeT scores were significantly increased in schizophrenia susceptibility genes in two consecutive age sets spanning 24–26 years.
source: To validate these results, we performed a series of technical control studies and biological replications. First, we used the DeGeT scoring system that showed the enrichment in schizophrenia peaked at 24–26 years (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The stronger enrichment seen with de novo mutations may reflect that GWAS detects common variants that are assumed to have lower penetrance.
source: Interestingly, the stronger enrichment seen with de novo mutations may reflect that GWAS detects common variants that are assumed to have lower penetrance (Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with citation to support the claim about GWAS variants.

claim: Schizophrenia-associated proteins were enriched in the mouse synapse proteins that changed prior to the 5 month peak (p=0.018, expected = 6, actual = 11).
source: Consistent with the transcriptome results, the mouse synapse proteomic dataset showed that schizophrenia-associated proteins were enriched in the synapse proteins that changed prior to the 5 month peak (p=0.018, expected = 6, actual = 11), and 91% of those that change were found to be down-regulated.
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance based on proteomic analysis.

claim: 91% of schizophrenia-associated proteins that changed in mouse synaptosomes were down-regulated.
source: Consistent with the transcriptome results, the mouse synapse proteomic dataset showed that schizophrenia-associated proteins were enriched in the synapse proteins that changed prior to the 5 month peak (p=0.018, expected = 6, actual = 11), and 91% of those that change were found to be down-regulated.
evidence: This is stated based on proteomic analysis.

claim: Schizophrenia genes were predominantly down-regulated prior to the TTTP.
source: We then examined the types of trajectories associated with schizophrenia and found genes were predominantly down-regulated prior to the TTTP (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Six proteins detected in mouse synaptosomes were associated with adult onset monogenic neurological disorders and were significantly enriched amongst proteins whose expression changed during maturation (p=0.00008, expected = 1, actual = 4).
source: We used the Human Phenotype Ontology age-of-onset annotations to identify these neurological disorders (excluding neoplasms, and peripheral/autonomic disorders) and from a total of 39 genes, six were detected in our samples, and we confirmed these were significantly enriched amongst the synapse proteins whose expression levels changed during maturation (p=0.00008, expected = 1, actual = 4, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: No equivalent enrichment was found for congenital/neonatal onset disorders in mouse synaptosomes (p=0.45, expected = 4, actual = 4).
source: No equivalent enrichment was found for congenital/neonatal onset disorders (p=0.45, expected = 4, actual = 4).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance as a control comparison.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in Atp2a2 cause Darier's disease and significantly increase the risk of many psychiatric disorders including mood disorders, depression, and schizophrenia.
source: Heterozygous mutations in Atp2a2 cause Darier's disease and significantly increase the risk of many psychiatric disorders including mood disorders, depression, and schizophrenia (Gordon-Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gordon-Smith et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations in Eef2 and Itpr1 cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 26 and 15/29, respectively.
source: Mutations in Eef2 and Itpr1 cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 26 and 15/29, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these genes.

claim: Atp1a3 mutations cause rapid-onset dystonia Parkinsonism, which leads to Parkinson's-like symptoms appearing during early adulthood, often with concurrent emergence of psychiatric symptoms.
source: Atp1a3 mutations cause rapid-onset dystonia Parkinsonism, which leads to Parkinson's-like symptoms appearing during early adulthood, often with concurrent emergence of psychiatric symptoms (Brashear et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brashear et al., 2012.

claim: Vcp mutations cause a form of frontotemporal dementia with a mean age of onset in the mid-thirties.
source: Vcp mutations cause a form of frontotemporal dementia with a mean age of onset in the mid-thirties (Watts et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watts et al., 2004.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in Atl1 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia with an age of onset around 21 years.
source: One of the main causes of hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) are heterozygous mutations in Atl1, which has an age of onset ~21 years (McCorquodale et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McCorquodale et al., 2011.

claim: Dmxl2 haploinsufficiency causes Polyendocrine-polyneuropathy syndrome.
source: Interestingly, we found that the synaptic scaffold protein Dmxl2 (haploinsufficiency causes Polyendocrine-polyneuropathy syndrome [Tata et al., 2014]) was reduced by ~70% (fold change: 0.28, p=0.00004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tata et al., 2014.

claim: Heterozygous deletion of Dmxl2 in central neurons delayed the onset of puberty in mice.
source: and studies in mice show heterozygous deletion of Dmxl2 in central neurons delayed the onset of puberty (Tata et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tata et al., 2014.

claim: None of the six other major brain disorders tested (autism, intellectual disabilities, multiple sclerosis, ALS, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's) showed significant enrichment in prefrontal cortex early adult turning points.
source: To address this we compiled gene lists for six other major brain disorders with different age-windows of onset: onset during infancy (autism and intellectual disabilities); early adulthood (multiple sclerosis); and late adulthood (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's) (corresponding gene sets shown in Supplementary file 1f). We applied the same bootstrapping approach used earlier for the PSD genes and none of the disorders showed significant results (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on the analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mammals with greatly differing lifespans share a conserved genomic program regulating the sequence of cellular and synaptic changes throughout the lifespan.
source: Thus, we conclude that mammals with greatly differing lifespans share a conserved genomic program regulating the sequence of cellular and synaptic changes throughout the lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of human and mouse data.

claim: The young adult brain undergoes a dramatic reorganisation of gene expression as revealed by the TTTP-peak around 26 years.
source: We discovered that the young adult brain undergoes a dramatic reorganisation of gene expression, as revealed by the TTTP-peak around 26 years, and this reorganisation is largely completed by 40 years of age when ninety percent of trajectories have plateaued.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the TTTP analysis.

claim: The reorganisation of gene expression in young adults is largely completed by 40 years of age when ninety percent of trajectories have plateaued.
source: We discovered that the young adult brain undergoes a dramatic reorganisation of gene expression, as revealed by the TTTP-peak around 26 years, and this reorganisation is largely completed by 40 years of age when ninety percent of trajectories have plateaued.
evidence: This is stated based on the cumulative TTTP analysis.

claim: Development and myelination in the frontal cortex is over by 40 years of age.
source: These findings correspond well with anatomical data showing that development and myelination in the frontal cortex is over (Lebel et al., 2012) by this age.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lebel et al., 2012.

claim: The TTTP-peak was enriched in neuronal and synaptic genes expressed in pyramidal and interneurons including those encoding PSD proteins and the 1.5 MDa PSD95 supercomplexes.
source: The TTTP-peak was enriched in neuronal and synaptic genes expressed in pyramidal and interneurons including those encoding PSD proteins and the 1.5 MDa PSD95 supercomplexes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: Young adults undergo a major reorganisation of their synapse proteomes.
source: This indicates that young adults undergo a major reorganisation of their synapse proteomes, which was supported by proteomics results in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptome and proteomic analyses.

claim: The level of expression of many PSD and PSD95 supercomplex proteins are known to be important for many innate and learned behaviours.
source: The level of expression of many PSD and PSD95 supercomplex proteins are known to be important for many innate and learned behaviours and we also found that the TTTP-peak was enriched in behaviourally important genes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with reference to the enrichment analysis.

claim: The genetic calendar can modify synapse proteome composition and potentially shape the behavioural repertoire across the lifespan.
source: Thus the genetic calendar can modify synapse proteome composition and potentially shape the behavioural repertoire across the lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about synaptic gene regulation and behavioral importance.

claim: The early age-window in endothelial cells corresponds to the expansion and maturation of the brain's vasculature.
source: The early age-window in endothelial cells corresponds to the expansion and maturation of the brain's vasculature (Caley and Maxwell, 1970; Engelhardt and Liebner, 2014; Azmitia et al., 2016) and post-natal shift in the transcriptome of endothelial cells (Daneman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on brain vasculature development.

claim: There was an enrichment in oligodendrocyte genes early in life, potentially corresponding to downregulation of genes specific to oligodendrocyte precursor cells.
source: There was also an enrichment in oligodendrocyte genes early in life, potentially corresponding to downregulation of genes specific to oligodendrocyte precursor cells (He et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to support the interpretation.

claim: The phase continuing through early teenage years involves strong upregulation of microglial genes and coincides with synaptic pruning.
source: The next phase, which continues through the early teenage years, involves strong upregulation of microglial genes and coincides with synaptic pruning (Schafer et al., 2012) and preceded the young adult window of synaptic and neuronal reorganisation.
evidence: This is stated with citation to support the connection to synaptic pruning.

claim: A genetic program orchestrating transcriptome trajectories causes reorganisation of expression of synapse proteins in young adults.
source: Our findings meet all five criteria and we propose the following model. A genetic program orchestrating transcriptome trajectories causes reorganisation of expression of synapse proteins in young adults.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the findings.

claim: Mutations in schizophrenia susceptibility genes are functionally exposed in young adults because the reorganisation of expression produces inappropriate synapse signalling properties that result in abnormal behaviour.
source: Mutations in these genes are functionally exposed in young adults because the reorganisation of expression produces inappropriate synapse signalling properties that result in abnormal behaviour.
evidence: This is part of the proposed genetic calendar model of schizophrenia.

claim: Schizophrenia is a genetic disorder targeting the mechanisms of brain aging during the young adulthood period of the lifespan.
source: This model posits that schizophrenia is a genetic disorder targeting the mechanisms of brain aging during the young adulthood period of the lifespan.
evidence: This is the core statement of the genetic calendar model of schizophrenia.

claim: The genetic calendar model can explain the onset and progression of schizophrenia.
source: Our model offers a mechanistic explanation for the onset of first-episode psychosis and is consistent with prodromal cognitive impairments and the persistence of schizophrenia beyond the young adult years (when many genes reach their plateau). Thus, the genetic calendar model can explain the onset and progression of schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the explanatory power of the proposed model.

claim: Amongst the schizophrenia-susceptibility genes with the most prominent TTTPs were Rgs4, Snap25, Kalrn, Htr2a and Nrg1.
source: Amongst the schizophrenia-susceptibility genes with the most prominent TTTPs were those with established synaptic functions, including Rgs4, Snap25, Kalrn, Htr2a and Nrg1.
evidence: This is stated based on the analysis of schizophrenia genes with high TTTP scores.

claim: The expression level of Rgs4, Snap25, Kalrn, Htr2a and Nrg1 has previously been shown to either influence, or be influenced by psychiatric symptoms.
source: The expression level of each of these genes has previously been shown to either influence, or be influenced by psychiatric symptoms (Etain et al., 2010; Guillozet-Bongaarts et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2013; Hill et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Altered expression of Snap25, Htr2a and Nrg1 are noted to associate with earlier age of onset of schizophrenia.
source: Furthermore, altered expression of Snap25, Htr2a and Nrg1 are noted to associate with earlier age of onset (Etain et al., 2010; Weickert et al., 2012; Abdolmaleky et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in Atp2a2 significantly increase the risk of mood disorders, depression, and schizophrenia.
source: Heterozygous mutations in Atp2a2 cause Darier's disease and significantly increase the risk of many psychiatric disorders including mood disorders, depression, and schizophrenia (Gordon-Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gordon-Smith et al., 2010.

claim: Rapid-onset dystonia Parkinsonism often presents with concurrent emergence of psychiatric symptoms.
source: Atp1a3 mutations cause rapid-onset dystonia Parkinsonism, which leads to Parkinson's-like symptoms appearing during early adulthood, often with concurrent emergence of psychiatric symptoms (Brashear et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brashear et al., 2012.

claim: The genetic lifespan calendar reduces expression below a critical threshold in young adults and is important for multiple neurological and psychiatric diseases.
source: These findings support the view that the genetic lifespan calendar reduces expression below a critical threshold in young adults and is important for multiple neurological and psychiatric diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of multiple neurological disorders.

claim: The genetic lifespan calendar is an innate mechanism that regulates the levels of postsynaptic proteins and hence changes the physiological and behavioural properties of brain circuits.
source: The genetic lifespan calendar is an innate mechanism that regulates the levels of postsynaptic proteins and hence changes the physiological and behavioural properties of brain circuits.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the function of the genetic calendar.

claim: The brain is not 'hard wired' but is continuously being modified by an evolutionary ancient and conserved genetic program.
source: This indicates that the brain is not 'hard wired' but is continuously being modified by an evolutionary ancient and conserved genetic program.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about the conserved genetic calendar.

claim: The postsynaptic proteins control innate and learned behaviours and thus the genetic calendar will modulate innate behaviours and the capacity to learn across the lifespan.
source: The postsynaptic proteins control innate and learned behaviours and thus the genetic calendar will modulate innate behaviours and the capacity to learn across the lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the known functions of postsynaptic proteins and the genetic calendar findings.

claim: The overarching biological function of the genetic calendar program could be to equip the animal for the challenges it faces at different ages.
source: The overarching biological function of this program could be to equip the animal for the challenges it faces at different ages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary function of the genetic calendar.

claim: Environmental triggers of psychosis, such as cannabis and other drugs of abuse, are known to act on the synaptic signalling mechanisms that are being reorganised in the TTTP-peak.
source: Interestingly, environmental triggers of psychosis, such as cannabis and other drugs of abuse, are known to act on the synaptic signalling mechanisms (Camp et al., 2011; Abbas et al., 2009) that are being reorganised in the TTTP-peak.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on drug effects on synaptic signaling.

claim: The enrichments in schizophrenia susceptibility genes in young adults was present even when fetal samples were not included in the analysis.
source: Our model also has implications for those schizophrenia models that posit a (non-genetic) fetal insult as the predisposing factor for later onset (Brown and Derkits, 2010): the enrichments in schizophrenia susceptibility genes in young adults was present even when fetal samples were not included in the analysis supporting the notion that it is a disorder of postnatal brain ageing.
evidence: This is stated based on the control analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: The identification of the conserved TTTP-peak between mice and humans may assist in refining animal models of adult-onset brain disorders.
source: The identification of the conserved TTTP-peak between mice and humans may also assist in refining animal models of adult-onset brain disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.
